claims.claim: Other EGFR Ex20Ins, such as the D770-N771insNPG, had a reduced affinity and sensitivity to EGFR TKIs.
claims.source: When studied in vitro, the EGFR Ex20Ins variant A763-Y764insFQEA was the only EGFR Ex20Ins-harboring cell line inhibited by erlotinib at concentrations less than 0.1 µM, while other EGFR Ex20Ins, such as the D770-N771insNPG, had a reduced affinity and sensitivity to EGFR TKIs (Yasuda et al., 2013; Hirano et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published experimental studies.

claims.claim: Mutagenesis studies indicate that the A763-Y764insFQEA insertion extends the αC-helix toward the N-terminal direction while the glutamic acid that is inserted through the mutation assumes the role of E762 in the WT-EGFR.
claims.source: Mutagenesis studies indicate that this insertion extends the αC-helix toward the N-terminal direction while the glutamic acid that is inserted through the mutation assumes the role of E762 in the WT-EGFR (Yasuda et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to published experimental studies.

claims.claim: The insertion in A763-Y764insFQEA leads to the replacement of I759 with alanine that has a shorter side chain.
claims.source: The insertion leads to the replacement of I759 with alanine that has a shorter side chain.
claims.evidence: This is structural knowledge based on the mutation.

claims.claim: In simulations of A763-Y764insFQEA initiated from the active conformation, the αC-helix transitioned back to the αC-in conformation several times after it visited the αC-out conformation.
claims.source: On the other hand, in the simulations that we initiated from the active conformation, the A763-Y764insFQEA was the only mutant in which the αC-helix transitioned back to the αC-in conformation several times after it visited the αC-out conformation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is data from the MD simulations performed in this study.

claims.claim: The intrinsic tendency of the A750-N756 segment of the N-terminal of the αC-helix to fold may restrict the conformational flexibility of the αC-helix and favor αC-in conformations in A763-Y764insFQEA.
claims.source: This unique behavior implies that the intrinsic tendency of the A750-N756 segment of the N-terminal of the αC-helix to fold that we see in the simulation may restrict the conformational flexibility of the αC-helix and favor αC-in conformations.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the MD simulation data.

claims.claim: The deepest minimum in the free energy landscape of A763-Y764insFQEA corresponds to an ensemble where the A-loop samples semi-closed conformations, but the αC-helix is stabilized in an αC-in conformation, where the K745-E762 salt bridge is formed.
claims.source: The deepest minimum in the free energy landscape of A763-Y764insFQEA – (CV1, CV2) = (−0.7, 0.3) – corresponds to an ensemble where the A-loop of the mutant samples semi-closed conformations, but unlike the WT, the αC-helix is stabilized in an αC-in conformation, where the K745-E762 salt bridge is formed (Figure 5, basin γ1).
claims.evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claims.claim: The activity of A763-Y764insFQEA has been found to be sensitive to Hsp90 inhibitors, suggesting that this mutant is dependent on Hsp90 for stability and downstream-signaling.
claims.source: In the case of the A763-Y764insFQEA, the activity of the mutant has been found to be sensitive to Hsp90 inhibitors, suggesting that this mutant is dependent on Hsp90 for stability and downstream-signaling (Jorge et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to published experimental studies.

claims.claim: The biological relevance of the observed elongated states with additional space between the two lobes in A763-Y764insFQEA might be to facilitate the recruitment of the Hsp90 chaperone.
claims.source: As the function of this mutant has been shown to be chaperone-dependent (Jorge et al., 2018), the biological relevance of the observed elongated states with additional space between the two lobes might be to facilitate the recruitment of the Hsp90 chaperone.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on simulation data and published experimental findings.

claims.claim: In the second main minimum of A763-Y764insFQEA, the mutant samples inactive conformations where the two-turn helix on the A-loop is formed and stabilized by interactions of K860 with the inserted glutamic acid, and the shifted E762 and E758, as well as of interaction of L858 with the inserted F764.
claims.source: In the second main minimum – (CV1, CV2) = (1.4, 0.1) – A763-Y764insFQEA samples inactive conformations where the two-turn helix on the A-loop is formed and stabilized by interactions of K860 with the inserted glutamic acid, and the shifted E762 and E758, as well as of interaction of L858 with the inserted F764 (Figure 5, basin γ2).
claims.evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claims.claim: The fully active state is populated in A763-Y764insFQEA, albeit there is a small thermodynamic penalty of 1–2 kcal mol−1 with respect to the inactive state.
claims.source: Notably, the fully active state is populated, albeit there is a small thermodynamic penalty of 1–2 kcal mol−1 with respect to the inactive state.
claims.evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claims.claim: In the apo, monomeric form of A763-Y764insFQEA, the insertion results in an extension of the 3 C loop, which seems to provide structural stability to the αC-helix.
claims.source: In the apo, monomeric form, the insertion results in an extension of the 3 C loop, which was expected to increase the mobility of the αC-helix. Instead, in both the unbiased and PTmetaD simulations that we performed, this extension seems to provide structural stability to the αC-helix.
claims.evidence: This is data from the MD and metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claims.claim: In both monomers of the asymmetric dimer of A763-Y764insFQEA, the αC-helix is kept predominately in the αC-in conformation.
claims.source: Moreover, looking at the position of the αC-helix in the two monomers of the asymmetric dimer, we see that, unlike the WT, the αC-helix is kept predominately in the αC-in conformation in both monomers (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is data from the MD simulations performed in this study.

claims.claim: EGFR mutants harboring ΔELREA show increased activity, comparable to the activity seen in L858R mutants and much higher than the one seen in the WT.
claims.source: EGFR mutants harboring ΔELREA show increased activity, comparable to the activity seen in L858R mutants and much higher than the one seen in the WT (Foster et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to published experimental studies.

claims.claim: Foster et al. showed that the deletion of five amino acids at the 3 C loop is optimal for kinase activation as this deletion is expected to prevent αC-helix from adopting an αC-out conformation.
claims.source: Foster et al. showed that the deletion of five amino acids at the 3 C loop is optimal for kinase activation as this deletion is expected to prevent αC-helix from adopting an αC-out conformation (Foster et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis from published literature.

claims.claim: ΔELREA EGFR is still oncogenic even in the absence of asymmetric homodimerization.
claims.source: Moreover, it has been recently shown that ΔELREA EGFR is still oncogenic even in the absence of asymmetric homodimerization (Cho et al., 2013), unlike the wild-type and L858R EGFR, which acquire their oncogenic properties following asymmetric dimerization.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to published experimental studies.

claims.claim: Wild-type and L858R EGFR acquire their oncogenic properties following asymmetric dimerization.
claims.source: Moreover, it has been recently shown that ΔELREA EGFR is still oncogenic even in the absence of asymmetric homodimerization (Cho et al., 2013), unlike the wild-type and L858R EGFR, which acquire their oncogenic properties following asymmetric dimerization.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to published experimental studies.

claims.claim: Modeling of the ΔELREA deletion in the active conformation suggests that the deletion does not significantly perturb the overall kinase domain.
claims.source: Modeling of the ΔELREA deletion in the active conformation suggests that the deletion does not significantly perturb the overall kinase domain.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from structural modeling performed in this study.

claims.claim: Modeling of the Src-like inactive conformation of ΔELREA suggests that unfolding of the turn at the N-terminal end of the αC-helix is necessary for it to adopt the characteristic αC-out conformation.
claims.source: On the other hand, modeling of the Src-like inactive conformation suggests that unfolding of this turn at the N-terminal end of the αC-helix is necessary for it to adopt the characteristic αC-out conformation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from structural modeling performed in this study.

claims.claim: Long unbiased molecular dynamics simulations by Shan et al. suggest that the ΔELREA mutation stabilizes the αC-in active conformation relative to the Src-like inactive conformation, but the mutation does not prevent αC-helix from sampling the αC-out conformation.
claims.source: Long unbiased molecular dynamics simulations by Shan et al. suggest that the ΔELREA mutation stabilizes the αC-in active conformation relative to the Src-like inactive conformation, but the mutation does not prevent αC-helix from sampling the αC-out conformation (Shan et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to published computational studies.

claims.claim: In unbiased simulations of ΔELREA, the αC-out is a stable conformation in terms of the structural integrity of the two-turn helix on the A-loop, the αC-helix and the overall folding of the receptor.
claims.source: In our unbiased simulations, we confirm that the αC-out is a stable conformation in terms of the structural integrity of the two-turn helix on the A-loop, the αC-helix and the overall folding of the receptor.
claims.evidence: This is data from the MD simulations performed in this study.

claims.claim: In one of the deepest free energy minima of ΔELREA, the characteristic two-turn helix on the A-loop of the Src-like inactive conformation is formed, and the αC-helix has shifted to adopt the αC-out conformation.
claims.source: The reconstructed free energy landscape confirms this observation, as the αC-helix is found in the αC-out conformation in one of deepest free energy minima – (CV1, CV2) = (1.4, 0.1) – the characteristic two-turn helix on the A-loop of the Src-like inactive conformation is formed, and the αC-helix has shifted to adopt the αC-out conformation (Figure 6, basin β2).
claims.evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claims.claim: The deleted L747 in ΔELREA is replaced by P753, and the stability of the Src-like inactive conformation is not compromised despite the deletion.
claims.source: The deleted L747, which on the WT contributes to the stabilization of the two-turn helix through a hydrophobic network between I759, L861, and L858 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), is replaced by P753 (Figure 6, basin β2) and, therefore, the stability of the Src-like inactive conformation is not compromised despite the deletion.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from structural analysis of simulation data.

claims.claim: In the second free energy minimum of ΔELREA, the mutant sampled mainly active-like conformations in which the αC-helix was in the αC-out conformation, but the A-loop assumed extended conformations.
claims.source: In the second free energy minimum – (CV1, CV2) = (1.6, 0.45) – ΔELREA sampled mainly active-like conformations in which the C was again in the αC-out conformation, but the A-loop assumed extended conformations (Figure 6, basin β1) similar to those seen in the unbiased simulations of the active WT-EGFR.
claims.evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claims.claim: The A-loop in ΔELREA also visited conformations in which the middle section of the A-loop formed a three-turn helix, reminiscent of an extended helix in the A-loop of MPSK1 kinase.
claims.source: Interestingly, the A-loop in this ensemble also visited conformations in which the middle section of the A-loop formed a three-turn helix, reminiscent of an extended helix in the A-loop of MPSK1 kinase (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, PDB ID: 2BUJ).
claims.evidence: This is data from the metadynamics simulations performed in this study.

claims.claim: The mutation in D770-N771insNPG possibly decouples the N/C-lobe motions and subsequently the coupling between the αC-helix and the A-loop and makes the transition to the inactive conformation less favorable.

claims.evidence: This is speculation based on simulation data and established knowledge.

claims.claim: Recent data show that the A763-Y764insFQEA insertion has greater sensitivity to agents such as gefitinib, erlotinib, and osimertinib.

results.result: EGFR kinase domain mutations are common oncogenic drivers in NSCLC. The most prevalent mutations are exon 19 deletions (45%), L858R in exon 21 (40-45%), and exon 20 insertions (4-10%). These mutations increase kinase activity (5-29 fold) and confer growth-factor-independent activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C16 establish well-documented background knowledge about EGFR mutations in NSCLC, supported by multiple citations to published literature. The prevalence statistics, mutation types, and fold-changes in catalytic activity are consistently reported across studies and provide essential context for the computational work.

results.result: The EGFR kinase domain structure consists of N- and C-lobes with key regulatory elements including the αC-helix, activation loop (A-loop), and conserved residues K745, E762, and D855. The A-loop adopts four main conformations (active, Src-like inactive, substrate competitive, detached), while the αC-helix transitions between αC-in (active) and αC-out (inactive) states.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C33 describe established structural features of EGFR kinase domain based on crystallographic data and prior computational studies. These are well-characterized aspects of kinase structure and regulation, supported by extensive literature citations and structural biology knowledge.

results.result: The αC-helix exhibits intrinsic disorder (partial unfolding) that is functionally important for EGFR signal propagation through asymmetric dimer formation. Phosphorylation of Y869 stabilizes the αC-helix and promotes EGFR multimerization.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 are supported by citations to prior MD simulations and H/D exchange experiments (Shan et al., 2012; Zanetti-Domingues et al., 2018). This establishes the functional importance of αC-helix disorder as a key regulatory mechanism in EGFR activation.

results.result: The study performed 36 µs of unbiased MD simulations using the a99SB-disp force field, which has been validated for simulating both folded and partially unfolded protein domains.
results.evaluation: Claims C39 and C115 describe the computational methodology. The total simulation time is clearly stated in Table 1, and the force field choice is justified by citation to validation studies (Robustelli et al., 2018). The methodology is appropriate for the research questions.

results.result: In unbiased MD simulations of apo, unphosphorylated WT-EGFR monomer starting from the active conformation, the αC-helix rapidly transitions to αC-out (~100 ns) but the A-loop remains extended, suggesting an energy barrier prevents formation of the Src-like inactive conformation. This indicates that dimerization, ATP binding, and phosphorylation are critical for stabilizing the active state.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C44 present simulation results consistent with known EGFR activation mechanisms. The observations are supported by simulation data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and align with prior computational studies (Shan et al., 2012). The inference about ATP/phosphorylation requirements (C44) is appropriately qualified as speculation.

results.result: In asymmetric WT-EGFR dimer simulations, the αC-helix is predominantly maintained in the αC-in conformation on the receiver monomer, while the activator monomer's αC-helix samples αC-out conformations. In symmetric dimers with both monomers in Src-like inactive conformation, both αC-helices remain in αC-out throughout simulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 are supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4. The differential behavior of receiver vs. activator monomers is consistent with the asymmetric activation mechanism of EGFR and provides computational validation of the dimerization-dependent activation model.

results.result: Metadynamics simulations of apo WT-EGFR reveal three main free energy minima corresponding to inactive-like conformations. The deepest minimum features a semi-closed A-loop and αC-out conformation. Secondary minima include a Src-like inactive state with the characteristic two-turn helix and partial αC-helix disorder.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 describe the free energy landscape from PTmetaD simulations (Figure 2). The results are consistent with prior metadynamics studies (Sutto and Gervasio, 2013) and support the notion that active conformations are energetically unfavorable in the absence of ligand/phosphorylation. The partial disorder of the αC-helix (C52) aligns with prior predictions.

results.result: L858R mutation stabilizes active-like conformations by creating favorable electrostatic interactions. R858 interacts with a cluster of negatively charged residues (E758, E762, D837, D855), stabilizing both the extended A-loop and the αC-helix structure. This suppresses the intrinsically disordered state and promotes EGFR dimerization.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C60 present a coherent mechanism for L858R activation supported by metadynamics simulations (Figure 3) and unbiased MD data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The electrostatic stabilization mechanism is structurally plausible and consistent with experimental observations of increased L858R activity and dimerization propensity (citations provided in C60).

results.result: For D770-N771insNPG, the inserted proline induces a turn creating a D770-R779 salt bridge observed in crystal structures. However, MD simulations show the K745-E762 salt bridge breaks immediately in apo simulations, suggesting the αC-in conformation in crystal structures is ligand-induced rather than mutation-induced.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C67 combine structural analysis with simulation data (Figures 4—figure supplements 1-2). The discrepancy between crystal structure and apo simulation behavior is clearly documented and leads to a reasonable inference (C67) that challenges prior hypotheses about this mutation's mechanism. The conclusion is appropriately qualified.

results.result: PTmetaD simulations of D770-N771insNPG show the A-loop predominantly adopts extended, active-like conformations even when the αC-helix is in the αC-out position. The mutation amplifies N/C-lobe separation in both monomeric and dimeric forms, potentially affecting substrate/inhibitor binding kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C72 are supported by metadynamics data (Figure 4) and unbiased simulations. The decoupling of A-loop and αC-helix conformations is a novel observation. The amplified lobe separation (C71-C72) is documented in simulations, though its functional significance remains speculative. The structural observations are sound.

results.result: A763-Y764insFQEA is uniquely sensitive to erlotinib among Ex20Ins mutations. The insertion extends the αC-helix N-terminally, with the inserted glutamate assuming E762's role. MD simulations show this mutant uniquely transitions back to αC-in conformation, suggesting the N-terminal αC-helix extension restricts conformational flexibility and favors αC-in states.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C78 combine experimental observations from literature (C73-C75) with simulation results (C77-C78, Figure 1—figure supplement 2). The unique reversibility to αC-in conformation is clearly documented in simulations and provides a structural rationale for the distinct TKI sensitivity. The inference about conformational restriction (C78) is reasonable.

results.result: The free energy landscape of A763-Y764insFQEA shows the deepest minimum corresponds to semi-closed A-loop with stabilized αC-in conformation. The fully active state appears as a low-energy secondary minimum. The mutation provides structural stability to the αC-helix and maintains αC-in conformation in both monomers of asymmetric dimers. Elongated states may facilitate Hsp90 chaperone recruitment.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C85 are supported by metadynamics simulations (Figure 5) and dimer simulations (Figure 1—figure supplement 4). The stabilization of αC-helix and accessibility of active states provides a mechanism for the mutation's activity. The Hsp90 recruitment hypothesis (C81) is appropriately speculative and supported by experimental citation (Jorge et al., 2018).

results.result: ΔELREA shows high catalytic activity comparable to L858R. Despite prior hypotheses that the deletion prevents αC-out conformations, simulations confirm αC-out is stable with intact Src-like inactive features. However, the deletion suppresses αC-helix disorder seen in WT. The free energy landscape shows multiple minima including Src-like inactive and active-like states with novel A-loop helical conformations. The mutation does not significantly alter the asymmetric dimer interface but suppression of αC-helix disorder should promote dimer formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C100 present a comprehensive analysis of ΔELREA combining literature data with extensive simulations (Figure 6). The key finding that αC-out conformations are accessible (C93-C94) challenges prior hypotheses (C87) and is well-supported by simulation data. The novel A-loop helical conformation (C97) is documented. The speculation about dimer promotion (C100) is reasonable given the disorder suppression.

results.result: The amplified lobe separation in D770-N771insNPG could explain low TKI sensitivity by affecting drug residence time. BDTX-189, structurally similar to neratinib, shows efficacy and likely binds αC-out conformations consistent with the mutation's free energy landscape. The mutation may decouple N/C-lobe motions and αC-helix/A-loop coupling.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C104 present reasonable hypotheses connecting simulation observations to TKI sensitivity, but lack direct validation. The lobe separation mechanism (C101) is speculative. The BDTX-189 binding mode inference (C103) is based on structural similarity without binding simulations. The decoupling hypothesis (C104) is plausible but not directly demonstrated. These require experimental validation.

results.result: A763-Y764insFQEA shows greater sensitivity to gefitinib, erlotinib, and osimertinib than other Ex20Ins. Simulations show the most stable apo conformation has αC-in with semi-closed A-loop, and the fully active state appears as a low-energy minimum. The mutation is predicted to promote asymmetric dimer formation through favorable interactions at the dimer interface (F760 in hydrophobic cleft, D761-K953 interaction).
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C110 combine experimental TKI sensitivity data (C105, cited) with simulation results (C106-C107, Figure 5) and structural analysis of the dimer interface (C109-C110, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The dimer promotion prediction (C108) is an inference from structural observations but is reasonable and testable.

results.result: The conformational ensembles from PTmetaD simulations showing extended conformations and open active sites can guide inhibitor design. Structural analysis suggests lapatinib (αC-out inhibitor) would clash with L858R but not A763-Y764insFQEA, while gefitinib fits better in L858R's tighter pocket.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C113 propose applications of the simulation data for drug design. While the structural observations about pocket differences are supported by simulation ensembles (Figure 7—figure supplement 5), the predictions about inhibitor selectivity (C112-C113) are inferences without binding calculations or experimental validation. These are reasonable hypotheses requiring further work.

results.result: The absence of intrinsically disordered αC-helix conformations in ΔELREA's free energy landscape could explain decreased sensitivity to lapatinib, as slow lapatinib binding kinetics are associated with transitions to partially unfolded αC-helix states.
results.evaluation: Claim C114 connects the suppression of αC-helix disorder in ΔELREA simulations to lapatinib resistance through a mechanism proposed in prior work (Shan et al., 2012). While the simulation observation is supported, the causal link to lapatinib sensitivity is speculative and appropriately qualified as such. Experimental validation would be needed.

results.result: Most Ex20Ins mutations render EGFR resistant to TKIs, with A763-Y764insFQEA being a notable exception.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38 establish the clinical motivation for studying these specific mutations. This is well-documented in the cited literature (Yasuda et al., 2012; Ward et al., 2021) and provides essential context for why the computational study focuses on comparing D770-N771insNPG and A763-Y764insFQEA.
